MicroCPipe is the smallest of the three pipelines and the one closest to what you build in the
course. If you only read one field guide page, read this one.

Code on this page is pulled from the repository at the pinned commit (253a6cc), and each
block links to the same lines on GitHub. Line numbers in the text are the file's own line numbers.

## What the pipeline does {#mc-biology}

Micro-C is a chromosome conformation capture assay. Cells are crosslinked, chromatin is digested
to single nucleosomes with micrococcal nuclease (MNase), and DNA ends that sat close together in
the nucleus are ligated to each other. After paired-end sequencing, each read pair is two pieces
of the genome that were near each other in 3D. Because MNase cuts between nucleosomes instead of
at restriction sites, the maps resolve structure down to the nucleosome scale.

The pipeline aligns both mates with `bwa mem -5SP -T0`, turns alignments into *pairs* with
`pairtools parse` (each pair gets a type: `UU` for two unique alignments, `UR`/`RU` for rescued
ones, and so on), sorts them, merges the sequencing runs of one library, marks duplicates, and
keeps only the unique pairs. Those pairs are binned into contact matrices in three formats: `.cool`,
a multi-resolution `.mcool`, and Juicebox `.hic`. Along the way it writes QC tables (pairtools stats,
cis/trans fractions, a preseq library-complexity curve) and one static HTML dashboard.

## The rule graph {#mc-rulegraph}

{{< generated name="microcpipe-rulegraph" >}}


Read it top to bottom. `align` feeds `dedup`; `dedup` feeds `split` and `qc_summary`; `split` feeds
`cool`, `hic` and `sort_bam`; `cool` feeds `mcool`; `sort_bam` feeds `library_complexity`. The maps
and QC tables feed `benchmark_summary` and `qc_report`. The optional `analysis_*` rules (on in the
test config, off by default) read the `.mcool` and feed nothing but `all`, so a failing analysis can
never block the dashboard. That last point is a design decision, not an accident: see
[Targets as functions](#mc-targets).

On the test fixture (three samplesheet rows, two libraries) a dry run plans 26 jobs: 3 `align`,
2 of each per-library rule, and one each of `benchmark_summary`, `qc_report` and `all`.

## A walk from inputs to outputs {#mc-walk}

1. **`MicroCSamplesheet.txt`** has one row per *sequencing run*. A library sequenced twice is two
   rows that differ only in `Seq_Rep`.
2. **`config/MicroCConfig.yaml`** says which columns identify a library (`mergeBy`), where the
   reference is, which map formats to make, and the QC thresholds.
3. **`MicroCPipe.sh`** picks a profile, makes a Python venv with Snakemake in it, and runs
   `snakemake -s workflows/MicroCPipe.snakefile --profile profiles/<site> ...`.
4. **`align`** runs once per row and writes a temporary `aligned/{run}.pairsam.gz`.
5. **`dedup`** runs once per library (`{group}`): it merges that library's runs and marks duplicates.
6. **`split`** writes `{group}.pairs.gz` (unique pairs only) and a BAM for preseq.
7. **`cool` → `mcool`** and **`hic`** build the maps from the pairs.
8. **`qc_summary`**, **`library_complexity`**, **`benchmark_summary`** and **`qc_report`** write the
   QC tables and `qc/MicroC_qc_report.html`.

Everything lands under `{outputDir}/{group}/`, including that library's `logs/` and `benchmarks/`.

## Concepts in the wild

### Runs and groups: two IDs from one samplesheet {#mc-run-group}

Module 3 builds sample names from samplesheet columns. MicroCPipe needs two names per row: one
for the alignment job (a sequencing run) and one for the library the run belongs to.

{{< snippet repo="microcpipe" file="workflows/MicroCPipe.snakefile" lines="15-35" >}}

- Lines 16-21 read the sheet with every column as a string (`dtype=str`; otherwise a `Bio_Rep` of
  `1` becomes the integer `1` and `"_".join` fails) and stop at parse time if a required column is
  missing. The required set includes whatever `mergeBy` names, so the check follows the config.
- Line 25 builds the library ID, `group`, by joining the `mergeBy` columns. Leave a column out of
  `mergeBy` and rows that differ only in that column become one group. The default leaves out
  `Seq_Rep`, which is how sequencing runs of one library end up merged.
- Line 27 builds the run ID from the group plus a counter (`cumcount`), so it is unique even when two
  rows have identical metadata. `align` needs that: one job per row, one output file per job.
- Lines 29-31 build three lookups the rules use: the ordered list of groups, the table indexed by run,
  and the runs of each group.
- Lines 33-35 are the part to copy. `wildcard_constraints` restricts `{group}` and `{run}` to the
  *actual* names from the samplesheet, joined with `|`. `re.escape` matters because sample names
  can contain regex characters: a `.` in `GM12878.ctrl` would otherwise match any character. With
  these constraints a typo in a target name fails right away with "no rule to produce", and
  Snakemake never has to guess where `{group}` ends and the rest of a filename begins.

### Input functions, and `{{group}}` inside `expand` {#mc-input-functions}

{{< snippet repo="microcpipe" file="workflows/MicroCPipe.snakefile" rule="dedup" >}}

The input of `dedup` is every run of this group. The list differs per group, so it has to be a
function of the wildcards (module 3). The interesting part is the double braces:

- `expand()` fills in `{run}` from `RUNS_BY_GROUP[w.group]`.
- `{{group}}` is an escaped brace. `expand()` turns it into a literal `{group}` instead of
  complaining that you did not give it a `group` list.
- Snakemake then fills `{group}` in the returned paths from the job's own wildcards. (Wildcards in
  strings returned by an input function are filled in, exactly like plain input strings.)

You could write `OUT + "/" + w.group + "/aligned/{run}.pairsam.gz"` instead and get the same paths.
The `{{group}}` form keeps the path looking like the `align` output it has to match, which makes
the connection easy to see. The `align` rule above it uses the simpler form of input function, one
lambda per file:

{{< snippet repo="microcpipe" file="workflows/MicroCPipe.snakefile" rule="align" >}}

Also look at the shell block: `: > {log}` empties the log once, then every command appends with
`2>> {log}`, so one log holds the whole pipe. Snakemake runs shell commands in bash strict mode
(`set -euo pipefail`), so if `bwa` dies in the middle of the pipe the job fails instead of writing a
truncated file. The `tmpdir` lives inside the group's output folder and is removed at the end.

### `rules.X.output` instead of retyping paths {#mc-rules-output}

{{< snippet repo="microcpipe" file="workflows/MicroCPipe.snakefile" rule="split" >}}

`split` takes its input from `rules.dedup.output.pairsam` (module 7). If someone renames the dedup
output, `split` follows. The rule also shows a pattern you will see again: an intermediate file
that is not an output (`{group}_all.pairs.gz`, passed as a `param`) is written and deleted inside
one job, so Snakemake never tracks it.

### A tool failure that is not a pipeline failure {#mc-preseq}

{{< snippet repo="microcpipe" file="workflows/MicroCPipe.snakefile" rule="library_complexity" >}}

preseq refuses to extrapolate a library that is too shallow or has too few duplicates. That says
something about the data, not about the pipeline, and the author did not want it to block the maps,
the dashboard or the Merge workflow. So:

- `preseq ... || { ...; }` runs the block in braces only if preseq fails. In bash, `{ ... }` groups
  commands without starting a subshell.
- In a Snakemake shell string, single braces are placeholders. A literal brace is written twice:
  `{{` and `}}` (module 4).
- The fallback warns on stderr and writes a header-only table, so the output exists, downstream
  rules run, and the dashboard shows "no data" for that library.
- Because of the `||`, strict mode does not stop the job when preseq fails. Without it, the job
  would fail and `--keep-going` would skip everything that depends on it.

The comment above the command explains *why*. That is the habit to copy: an `||` that swallows an
error needs a sentence saying which error and why it is safe.

### Resources live only in profiles {#mc-resources}

{{< snippet repo="microcpipe" file="workflows/rules/common.smk" lines="1-3" >}}

Rules in MicroCPipe declare `threads:` and nothing else. Memory, runtime and partition come from
the site profile:

{{< snippet repo="microcpipe" file="profiles/slurm-template/config.yaml" lines="1-27" >}}

- `default-resources` covers any rule without its own entry; `set-threads` and `set-resources`
  (further down the file) give every rule by name.
- `cores: 100` is there for a reason the comment spells out: without it, Snakemake capped a rule's
  `threads` at the CPUs of the small launcher job, and `align` ran with 3 threads instead of 16.
- `latency-wait: 500` is how long Snakemake waits for an output file to appear after a job ends.
  On a shared cluster file system, a file written on a compute node can take a while to be visible
  from the node where Snakemake runs; without enough wait, a job that succeeded is reported as
  "missing output". The local profile uses 60 seconds.
- The `<account>` placeholders are checked by the launcher (next section) so an unedited template
  stops with a clear message instead of a SLURM error.

The benefit: moving to a new cluster means copying one folder, not editing rules. The cost: every
rule name appears in five profiles, so adding a rule means five edits. See
[conventions](conventions.qmd#resources) for a way to keep the per-rule numbers in one place.

One rule reads its resources back. `hic` sizes the Java heap from the memory the profile gave it:

{{< snippet repo="microcpipe" file="workflows/rules/formats.smk" rule="hic" >}}

`params.mem` is a function of `wildcards` and `resources`. It takes 85% of `mem_mb` (Java needs
room outside the heap), unless the config sets `javaMem`. Raising `hic: mem_mb` in a profile is
enough; nobody has to remember to change a second number.

### The launcher, and why it does not activate the venv {#mc-launcher}

{{< snippet repo="microcpipe" file="MicroCPipe.sh" lines="32-85" >}}

- Lines 36-45: `--configfile` and `--profile` are read by the script; every other argument goes to
  Snakemake unchanged, so `bash MicroCPipe.sh -n` is a dry run.
- Lines 48-50: the profile is `--profile`, else `$MICROC_PROFILE`, else `hpcProfile` from the
  config. The environment variable lets each person set their cluster once in `~/.bashrc` and keep
  the repository cluster-neutral.
- Lines 59-63 stop early on an unedited `<placeholder>`.
- Lines 73-74 create `env/` and install Snakemake into it, but **never run `source env/bin/activate`**.
  The comment explains why: conda rewrites a tool's first line to `#!/usr/bin/env python3` when the
  environment path is longer than Linux's 127-character limit (common on scratch file systems).
  If a venv's `bin/` were first on `PATH` inside jobs, that line would find the venv's Python, which
  does not have the tool's packages, and the job would fail with `No module named ...`. Calling
  `env/bin/python3 -m snakemake` directly keeps the venv off `PATH`.
- Lines 78-82 add SLURM log and rate-limit flags only when the profile uses the SLURM executor.
- Line 85: `--rerun-incomplete --keep-going -p` are always on. After a crash, half-written files are
  redone; one failed library does not stop the others; and the log shows each shell command.

The same idea shows up inside the rules. Scripts are run with `$CONDA_PREFIX/bin/python`, the
interpreter of the rule's own conda environment, not whatever `python` comes first on `PATH`:

{{< snippet repo="microcpipe" file="workflows/MicroCPipe.snakefile" lines="180-195" >}}

`{workflow.basedir}/../scripts/` finds the script relative to the Snakefile, not to the directory you
launched from.

### Targets as functions {#mc-targets}

{{< snippet repo="microcpipe" file="workflows/MicroCPipe.snakefile" lines="51-68" >}}

`rule all` asks for whatever the config switches turn on. `qc_targets()` adds the preseq table only
when both `library_complexity` and `make_bam` are true, because preseq reads the BAM. The map
targets come from `format_targets()` in `common.smk`, which adds one `.done` file per requested
analysis. Those markers are made with Snakemake's `touch()` output flag next to the real result
(see `analysis_expected` in `formats.smk`). Note that `qc_report` asks for `map_targets()`, not
`format_targets()`: the dashboard waits for the maps but not for the optional analyses.

### Config checked at parse time {#mc-validation}

{{< snippet repo="microcpipe" file="workflows/rules/common.smk" lines="8-18" >}}

These lines run when the Snakefile is read, before any job exists. A typo in `outputs:` or a
resolution that is not a multiple of the base stops the run with one readable line. The dry-run
test `test_bad_output_format_is_rejected` checks the first of these.

### One rule file, two workflows {#mc-include}

`rules/formats.smk` holds the map rules (`cool`, `mcool`, `hic`, `analysis_*`) and is included by
both the core workflow and `MicroCMerge.snakefile`. It needs to know where the pairs file is, and
that differs between the two. The answer is a hook function that each Snakefile defines before the
include:

{{< snippet repo="microcpipe" file="workflows/MicroCPipe.snakefile" lines="263-267" >}}

{{< snippet repo="microcpipe" file="workflows/MicroCMerge.snakefile" lines="67-72" >}}

`formats.smk` uses `pairs = get_pairs` as an input function. The `merged_` prefix on merge groups
keeps their files from colliding with core groups in the same output folder:

{{< snippet repo="microcpipe" file="workflows/MicroCMerge.snakefile" lines="21-27" >}}

This is a hand-made version of what Snakemake's `module`/`use rule ... with:` system does. It works
with plain `include:`, which is easier to read at this size.

### Notifications from `onstart`/`onsuccess`/`onerror` {#mc-hooks}

{{< snippet repo="microcpipe" file="workflows/MicroCPipe.snakefile" lines="37-49" >}}

These hooks run once, in the main Snakemake process, and not on a dry run. `notify()` (in
`common.smk`) sends one email per event if an address is set, and wraps the send in `try`/`except`
so a broken mail setup can never fail a finished run. In `onerror`, `log` is the path of
Snakemake's own log, and `log_tail()` puts its last 40 lines in the message.

### Dry-run tests that count jobs {#mc-tests}

{{< snippet repo="microcpipe" file="tests/test_dryrun.py" lines="19-39" >}}

`tests/dryrun/` holds a tiny fixture: three samplesheet rows (two runs of one library, one run of a
second), empty FASTQs, and a config that overlays the main one. The test runs `snakemake -n` and
reads the job table. Three rows must give three `align` jobs and two `dedup` jobs. If someone
breaks the run/group logic, the counts change and CI fails. CI (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`) also
runs `bash -n` on the launchers so a syntax error in a shell script is caught before it reaches a
cluster.

## What you would change {#mc-change}

- **Put `Condition` in `mergeBy`.** The samplesheet has a `Condition` column, but the default
  `mergeBy` is `Project`, `Cell_Type`, `Bio_Rep`, `Tech_Rep`. A control and a treated library with the
  same replicate numbers would become one group and be merged. Either add `Condition` or make the
  parse-time check refuse a group whose rows disagree on `Condition`.
- **Pass all config files to the dashboard.** `qc_report` gives the script
  `workflow.configfiles[0]`, so a threshold changed in a second `--configfile` is not seen by the
  dashboard. TTpipe passes them all (`QC_CONFIGFILES` in `report.smk`).
- **Use f-strings for paths.** `OUT + "/{group}/..."` is the source of most of the lint output (see
  [conventions](conventions.qmd#lint)). `f"{OUT}/{{group}}/..."` reads the same and lints clean.
- **Keep per-rule numbers in one file.** See [conventions](conventions.qmd#resources).

## Exercises for the curious {#mc-exercises}

1. You want one map per biological replicate *and* one map that pools both biological replicates.
   What would you change, and do you need to rerun alignment?
2. Why does `dedup` merge the runs of a library first and mark duplicates after, instead of
   deduplicating each run on its own?
3. You need `hic` to get 200 GB on one cluster only. Which file do you edit, and why does the Java
   heap follow without a second edit?
4. Remove `re.escape` from the constraints and name a library `K562.ctrl`. What could go wrong?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Short answers

1. No realignment. Write a merge samplesheet that lists each library's `{group}.pairs.gz` and set
   `merge.mergeBy` to the columns that stay fixed when you pool, for example `['Project',
   'Cell_Type', 'Condition']` (no `Bio_Rep`, no `Tech_Rep`). Run `MicroCMerge.sh`. It only runs
   `merge_pairs` and the format rules.
2. A PCR duplicate is a copy of the same ligation product, and copies of one library can be read
   in different sequencing runs. Deduplicating per run would miss duplicates that span runs.
   Libraries are not deduplicated against each other (Merge does not dedup), because two
   libraries cannot share PCR copies.
3. `set-resources: hic: mem_mb:` in that site's `profiles/<site>/config.yaml`. `params.mem` in
   `hic` is computed from `resources.mem_mb` (85% of it) unless `javaMem` is set in the config.
4. The `.` becomes a regex "any character", so the constraint also accepts `K562Xctrl` or
   `K562_ctrl`. With similar library names, a pattern could match a name you did not mean, and the
   constraint no longer guarantees that a target names a real library. `re.escape` makes each name
   match only itself.
:::
